evidence_quotes.quote: We used this framework to carry out an inductive analysis by comparing water service delivery and governance in four small towns across two states (Karnataka and Tamil Nadu) in southern India.

In terms of the institutional arrangements for water service delivery: the towns in Tamil Nadu (Kannampalayam and Palladam) receive bulk supply of river water from a provincial para-statal agency, Tamil Nadu Water and Drainage Board (TWAD Board), but manage the distribution of this river and of GW on their own.
Third, in terms of charging for water supply, the supply at the public standpipes is free of charge, whereas in-house connections are charged at a fixed (unmetered) monthly rate.

Drawing upon data gathered from household surveys, interviews, physical measurement of borewell pumping rates, and secondary data, we seek to understand what might be the appropriate role for different state agencies and how different sources of water might be optimally used, at the same time pointing to the influence of other factors outside the service modality.

In terms of affordability, the cost at which water is supplied varies from 0 (for public standpipes) to a fixed charge for in-house connections that varies from 50 Rs/month (Kannampalayam), 80 Rs/month (Nelamangala), 100 Rs/month (Palladam) and 120 Rs/month (Ramanagara)

All towns have responded to socio-economic inequality through the concept of free supply at public standpipes, and increasing the density of such standpipes in the poorer neighbourhoods – but the town with the para-statal has done the poorest job here.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines domestic water service delivery and household/community water access (in-house connections, public standpipes, water quantity supplied and consumed, supply frequency, and affordability) in four small towns in southern India.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it directly compares institutional and governance arrangements for urban water supply (elected Urban Local Bodies vs. provincial engineering para-statal agencies TWAD Board and KUWSDB). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines utility ownership/institutional-regulatory structure governing retail water distribution versus bulk supply, tariff and cost-recovery rules (free public standpipe rules vs. fixed unmetered monthly tariffs for in-house connections and municipal fee-recovery enforcement), connection moratoria/illegal connection practices, and frontline grievance/accountability mechanisms shaping household access.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical comparative mixed-methods study combining household source-mix surveys (N = 300 in Nelamangala; N = 600 in Ramanagara), household volumetric metering (N = 5 and N = 8), standpipe pot-collection surveys (N = 41), semi-structured interviews with households (>20 per town), linemen, municipal staff, councillors, and para-statal engineers, physical borewell discharge measurements, and municipal/utility administrative and financial records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes including per-capita water supply and household consumption (lpcd), share of households with in-house connections versus standpipe dependence, supply frequency/continuity across normal and summer seasons, public standpipe density in low-income neighbourhoods, affordability (monthly connection charges and Rs/m3), and perceived water quality.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and multi-level units of analysis (four small towns in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, wards, and surveyed/monitored households), exposure (institutional service delivery structure: ULB vs. ULB + provincial para-statal vs. para-statal alone, tariff/cost-recovery rules, and dual-sourcing rules), outcomes (adequacy/lpcd, connection vs. standpipe use, continuity/frequency, affordability, equity, sustainability, and responsiveness), and study design (comparative mixed-methods empirical case study).

study_design: Comparative mixed-methods empirical case study (household surveys, household metering, borewell flow measurements, administrative/financial records, and semi-structured interviews)
population_and_sample: Four small towns (populations ~15,868 to ~95,167) in Karnataka (Nelamangala, Ramanagara) and Tamil Nadu (Kannampalayam, Palladam), India; multi-level analysis at town, ward, and household levels including household surveys (N = 300 in Nelamangala; N = 600 in Ramanagara), household volumetric metering (N = 5 and N = 8), standpipe pot survey (N = 41), and >20 semi-structured household interviews plus staff/councillor interviews per town (2014–15 data).
exposure: Institutional utility structure and water service modalities: municipal (Urban Local Body) distribution alone vs. provincial para-statal bulk supply with municipal distribution vs. full para-statal supply and distribution, alongside tariff/cost-recovery rules (free public standpipes vs. fixed monthly connection charges) and dual-sourcing rules (surface water plus groundwater vs. groundwater only).
outcome: Domestic water adequacy/quantity (town and household lpcd), in-house connection vs. public standpipe dependence, supply frequency/continuity in normal and summer months, standpipe density in low-income areas, affordability (Rs/month and Rs/m3), perceived water quality, financial cost recovery, biophysical sustainability, and agency responsiveness/accountability.
rationale: This comparative mixed-methods empirical study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It empirically examines how utility institutional/ownership structures (local elected municipal bodies vs. provincial engineering para-statals TWAD Board and KUWSDB for bulk supply and retail distribution) and tariff/cost-recovery rules (free standpipes vs. fixed monthly connection tariffs and fee enforcement) directly govern domestic water access, supply frequency, household lpcd, standpipe density in poorer areas, affordability, and grievance redressal across four small towns in southern India.
